note: Drafted by the chat assistant 11-03 for the owner's review (D150 P1). Nothing is live until approved in Admin → Learn → Questions. 'pieces' are suggested Learn step ids to verify.

items.stem: Your daily revenue job runs at 00:30. Mobile events can arrive up to 48 hours late, and finance says yesterday's numbers keep changing after they report them. What do you change?
choices: Aggregate by event time with a watermark, and idempotently reprocess the last two days' partitions on each run
Drop events that arrive after the job has run
Aggregate by the time events arrive instead of when they happened
Move the job to 03:00 so more events have arrived
why: Event time keeps each sale on the right day, and reprocessing a fixed window idempotently makes late data land correctly without duplicates. Finance can be told when a day is final.
That loses real revenue; the report becomes stable but wrong.
Stable, but it attributes sales to the wrong day, which is worse for finance.
Three hours doesn't cover a 48-hour delay; the numbers will still move.

items.stem: Your Kafka-to-warehouse loader writes duplicate rows whenever a consumer restarts. What's the fix?
choices: Use larger batches so restarts happen less often
Turn off auto-commit and change nothing else
Increase the consumer's retry count
Write with an upsert / merge keyed on the event id, and commit offsets only after the write succeeds
why: Fewer restarts, same bug; each restart still duplicates a larger batch.
Manual commits help ordering, but a crash between write and commit still replays the batch, so you still need idempotent writes.
More retries mean more chances to write the same event twice.
Idempotent writes make a replay harmless, and committing after the write means nothing is skipped: effectively exactly-once into the warehouse.

items.stem: Analysts query a 2 TB fact table, almost always filtered by date and then by customer. Queries take minutes. What do you do first?
choices: Split the table into one table per customer
Partition by date and cluster (or sort) by customer
Add an index on every column
Add more warehouse nodes
why: Thousands of tables are unmanageable and break every cross-customer query.
Partitioning lets the engine skip whole dates, and clustering by customer makes the remaining scan small. It matches how the table is actually queried.
Most warehouses are columnar and don't use row indexes this way; it adds write cost for little gain.
Costs more and helps a little, but every query still scans data it doesn't need.

items.stem: An upstream team renamed a field without warning and your pipeline silently loaded nulls for a week. How do you stop this happening again?
choices: Pin your pipeline to the old schema permanently
Agree a data contract with a schema registry and compatibility rules, and fail fast in staging when a change breaks it
Ask the upstream team to email you before changes
Wrap the parser in try/catch and skip rows that fail
why: The upstream data will keep changing; you'd just break later and harder.
A contract with enforced compatibility makes breaking changes visible before they reach production, and failing fast turns a silent week into a loud minute.
Helpful, but it relies on memory. Nothing enforces it.
Skipping rows hides the problem; you'd lose data silently instead of loading nulls silently.

items.stem: You need to backfill three years of history into a table that dashboards read all day. How do you run it?
choices: Truncate the table and reload everything in one go
One large job over the whole range, overnight
Run it on the production cluster at peak, so it finishes fastest
In date-partition chunks, idempotently, with bounded parallelism and a row-count check per chunk
why: The dashboards show an empty or half-filled table while it reloads.
If it fails at 80% you start again, and it may still be running when the dashboards are busy.
It competes with the readers you're trying to protect.
Chunks can be retried one at a time, idempotency makes reruns safe, bounded parallelism protects the dashboards, and counts prove each chunk is complete.

items.stem: A dashboard suddenly shows a spike in nulls in a key column. What should have caught this before anyone saw it?
choices: A fix in the BI layer that hides nulls
Nothing: dashboards are where you notice problems
Expectations at ingestion that check nulls, ranges and volumes, alert on failure, and quarantine bad batches
A full reload of the table every night
why: Hiding nulls makes the dashboard look fine while the data is wrong.
Your users become your monitoring, which costs trust.
Checks where data enters catch problems at the source, and quarantine stops bad data spreading downstream while you fix it.
Reloads repeat the same bad data.

items.stem: Two withdrawal requests for the same account arrive at the same moment, and both pass the 'enough balance?' check. The account goes negative. What's the fix?
choices: Retry the request if anything fails
Check the balance again just before updating, in the application
Do it in one atomic step: a conditional update (UPDATE … SET balance = balance − x WHERE balance ≥ x) or a row lock inside a transaction
Cache the balance so reads are faster
why: Retries don't prevent two successful withdrawals.
Two checks still race; the gap between check and update is the bug.
The database makes check-and-update one atomic step, so only one of two concurrent requests can succeed.
Faster reads make the race more likely, not less.

items.stem: Mobile clients retry when a request times out, and some customers now have two identical orders. What do you add?
choices: A nightly job that deletes duplicates
Longer request timeouts
Turn off retries in the app
Idempotency keys: the client sends a unique key per order, and the server returns the first result for a repeated key
why: Customers have already been charged twice by then.
Timeouts still happen on bad networks; the duplicate just takes longer to appear.
Customers then see failures for orders that actually went through.
The server recognises a retry of the same order and returns the original result, so retries become safe.

items.stem: An endpoint that lists 50 orders makes 51 database queries, one per order for its items, and its p95 latency is climbing. What do you change?
choices: Cache every response forever
Load the items in one batched query (a join or an IN query) instead of one per order
Increase the database connection pool
Add more application servers
why: Stale data, and the first request is still slow.
One query instead of 51 removes the N+1 pattern, and latency drops with it.
More connections let more of the slow pattern run at once.
The database still does 51 round trips per request; more servers can make it worse.

items.stem: When a hot cache key expires, thousands of requests miss at once and hammer the database. What prevents this?
choices: A shorter TTL
A bigger cache
Remove the cache
Let one request refresh the key while the others wait or get the slightly stale value, with jittered TTLs so keys don't expire together
why: Expiry happens more often, so the stampede happens more often.
Size doesn't help: the problem is many requests for the same expired key.
Every request goes to the database all the time.
Request coalescing (or stale-while-revalidate) turns thousands of misses into one refresh, and jitter spreads expiries out.

items.stem: Three other teams use your REST API. A response field has to change from a string to an object. How do you ship it?
choices: Create a brand-new endpoint for every change
Ask each team to deploy at exactly the same time as you
Change it in place and tell the teams afterwards
Add the new shape alongside the old (or version the endpoint), announce a deprecation window, and remove the old shape only when usage drops to zero
why: It works once, then leaves a maze of endpoints to maintain.
Coordinated deploys across teams fail in practice.
Their integrations break the moment you deploy.
Additive changes and versioning let clients move at their own pace, and measuring usage tells you when it's safe to remove the old shape.

items.stem: Your service calls a payments provider that sometimes hangs for 30 seconds. During incidents, your whole service becomes unresponsive. What's the design fix?
choices: Short timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, a circuit breaker, and a fallback (queue the payment, tell the user it's processing)
Increase the server's thread pool
Retry failed calls until they succeed
Call the provider from more threads in parallel
why: Timeouts stop slow calls tying up your service, the breaker stops calling a provider that's down, and the fallback keeps users moving. The failure stays contained.
A bigger pool just takes a little longer to fill up with hung calls.
Infinite retries pile more load onto a provider that's already struggling.
More concurrent hung calls exhaust resources faster.

items.stem: Your model scored well offline but performs poorly in production on the same kind of data. What do you check first?
choices: Training/serving skew: are the features computed the same way, with the same data, at training and at serving time?
Train for more epochs
Whether a bigger model would do better
Lower the decision threshold
why: The most common cause is features computed differently online and offline (a different code path, missing joins, stale data). Comparing the two directly usually finds it.
The offline score was already good; this isn't underfitting.
If the inputs differ, a bigger model learns the wrong thing better.
It hides the symptom and shifts errors around.

items.stem: A fraud model reports 99.5% accuracy, but only 0.5% of transactions are fraud. How should you evaluate it?
choices: Report ROC-AUC only
Accuracy is fine at 99.5%
Use precision and recall (and PR-AUC) on the fraud class, and choose the threshold by the cost of missed fraud versus false alarms
Oversample to 50/50 and report accuracy on that
why: ROC-AUC can look strong on very imbalanced data while precision is poor; PR-AUC is more telling here.
Predicting 'never fraud' scores 99.5% and catches nothing.
Precision and recall measure what matters for a rare class, and a cost-based threshold ties the model to the business decision.
Accuracy on a resampled set doesn't reflect the real-world mix.

items.stem: Your app calls an LLM on every request. Many users ask near-identical questions, p95 latency is 8 seconds, and the bill has tripled. What do you build?
choices: Cap the output length and nothing else
Turn the feature off until costs settle
An inference layer in front of the model: cache exact and near-duplicate answers, route easy requests to a smaller model, and fall back gracefully when the provider is slow
Switch every request to a smaller, cheaper model
why: Helps cost a little; doesn't touch repeated work or latency spikes.
Solves the bill by removing the product.
Caching removes repeated work, routing spends the big model only where it matters, and fallbacks protect latency. It fixes cost, speed and reliability together.
Cheaper, but quality drops for the hard requests that need the larger model.

items.stem: Your first model scores 0.98 AUC on validation, far above anything you expected. What's the right next step?
choices: Tune the hyperparameters further
Check for leakage: features that wouldn't exist at prediction time, and a random split where a time-based split is needed
Ship it
Add regularisation
why: Tuning a leaky model makes the leak fit better.
Leakage, such as features computed after the outcome or future data in training, is the usual cause. A time-based split shows the real performance.
A score too good to be true usually is; production will expose it.
Regularisation doesn't remove information that shouldn't be there.

items.stem: Three months after launch, your model's business results are slipping, but latency and error rates look fine. What should have been in place?
choices: Latency and error monitoring only
Monitoring of input distributions and of model performance as labels arrive, with alerts, plus a retraining process evaluated in shadow before it replaces the live model
Never retrain; the model was validated at launch
Automatic retraining every day, regardless
why: Those only tell you the service is up, not whether the model is still right.
Watching the inputs (drift) and the outcomes (performance) catches decay early, and shadow evaluation makes retraining safe.
The world changes after launch; static models decay.
Blind retraining can bake in bad data and hides why things changed.

items.stem: You need to serve a 7-billion-parameter model on a single GPU. It barely fits, throughput is poor, and long prompts run out of memory. What do you do first?
choices: Add more replicas without changing the model
Raise the batch size and nothing else
Move inference to the CPU
Quantise the weights (e.g. 8-bit or FP8), manage the KV cache (paged or capped by context length), and batch requests dynamically
why: Each replica has the same memory problem, and the cost multiplies.
Bigger batches need more memory, which is exactly what's running out.
Far slower for a model this size.
Quantisation shrinks the weights, KV-cache management stops long prompts exhausting memory, and dynamic batching keeps the GPU busy. Memory and throughput improve together.
